exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Second Moment of a Random Variable

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{3}{x^4}, \quad x \geq 1. \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^2].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of $X^2$ is given by

\[ \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_{S} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

We compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows:

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^2] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{3}{x^4} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} 3x^{-2} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left. -\dfrac{3}{x} \right|_{1}^{\infty} \\[5pt] &= -\left(0 - \dfrac31\right) \\[5pt] &= 3 \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

\[ f(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{x^2}, & 1 < x \leq 2, \\[5pt] \dfrac{x}{5}, & 2 \leq x < 3. \end{cases} \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^2].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of $X^2$ is given by

\[ \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_{S} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows:

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^2] &= \int_{1}^{3} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{2} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x + \int_{2}^{3} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{x}{5} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{2} \,\textrm{d}x + \int_{2}^{3} \dfrac{x^3}{5} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= x \,\bigg|_{1}^{2} + \left. \dfrac{x^4}{20} \right|_{2}^{3} \\[5pt] &= (2 - 1) + \left( \dfrac{81}{20} - \dfrac{16}{20} \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 + \dfrac{13}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{17}{4} \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \dfrac{1}{8}\,x, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 4. \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^2].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of $X^2$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_{S} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

We compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^2] & = \int_{0}^{4} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{8}\,x \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8}\int_{0}^{4} x^3 \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{32}\, x^4 \, \Bigg|_{0}^{4} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{32}\left(256 - 0\right)\\[5pt] & = 8 \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x)= \begin{cases} x, & 0 < x \lt 1, \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{3}\,x, & 1 \leq x < 2. \end{cases} \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^2].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of $X^2$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_{S} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^2] & = \int_{0}^{2} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^2 \cdot x \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{2} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\,x \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^3 \, \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{1}{3}\int_{1}^{2} x^3 \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4} \,x^4 \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} + \dfrac{1}{12}\,x^4 \, \Bigg|_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(1 - 0\right) + \dfrac{1}{12}\left(16 - 1\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{5}{4}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{2}. \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x)= \begin{cases} x^2, & 0 < x \lt 1, \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{x^2}, & 1 \leq x < 3. \end{cases} \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^2].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of $X^2$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_{S} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^2] & = \int_{0}^{3} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^2 \cdot x^2 \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{3} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^2} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^4 \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{3} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{5}\, x^5 \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} + x \, \Bigg|_{1}^{3} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{5}\left(1 - 0\right) + \left(3 - 1\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{5} + 2\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{11}{5}. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Higher Moments of a Random Variable

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{4}, & 0 \leq x \lt 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{x^5}, & x \geq 1. \end{cases} \]

Calculate $\textrm E [X^3].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_{S} x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^3] & = \int_{0}^{\infty} x^3 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^3 \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \,\textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{\infty} x^3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^5}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{4}\int_{0}^{1} x^3 \, \textrm{d}x + \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{1}^{a} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{16}\,x^4 \,\Bigg|_{0}^{1} + \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(- \dfrac{1}{x}\right) \Bigg|_{1}^{a} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{16}\left(1 - 0\right) + \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(1- \dfrac{1}{a}\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{16} + (1-0)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{19}{16} \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x)= \begin{cases} x^3, & 0 \leq x \lt 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\,x, & 1 \leq x \leq 2. \end{cases} \]

Calculate $\textrm E [X^4].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_{S} x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the fourth raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^4] & = \int_{0}^{2} x^4 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^4 \cdot x^3 \,\textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{2} x^4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\,x \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^7 \, \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{2} x^5 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8}\,x^8 \,\Bigg|_{0}^{1} + \dfrac{1}{12}\,x^6 \, \Bigg|_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(1 - 0\right) + \dfrac{1}{12}\left(64 - 1\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{21}{4}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{43}{8} \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x)= \begin{cases} 1-x^2, & 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{8}{9x^3}, & 1 \lt x \leq 2. \end{cases} \]

Calculate $\textrm E [X^3].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_{S} x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^3] & = \int_{0}^{2} x^3 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^3 \cdot (1-x^2) \,\textrm{d}x + \int_{1}^{2} x^3 \cdot \dfrac{8}{9x^3}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} (x^3 - x^5) \, \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{8}{9} \int_{1}^{2} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\,x^4 - \dfrac{1}{6}\,x^6 \right) \Bigg|_{0}^{1} + \dfrac{8}{9}\,x \, \Bigg|_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{6} - 0\right) + \dfrac{8}{9}\left(2 - 1\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{8}{9}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{35}{36} \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = 2x, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 1. \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^4].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_{S} x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the fourth raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^4] & = \int_{0}^{1} x^4 \cdot 2x \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2 \int_{0}^{1} x^5 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}\,x^6 \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - 0\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3} \end{align}

question.text:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function \[ f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2x}, \quad 1 \leq x \leq e^2. \]

Calculate $\textrm{E}[X^4].$
question.explanation:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_{S} x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the fourth raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align} \textrm{E}[X^4] & = \int_{1}^{e^2} x^4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{e^2} x^3 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8}\,x^4 \, \Bigg|_{1}^{e^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8}\left( e^8 - 1\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^8 - 1}{8} \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Mean of a Transformed Random Variable

question.text:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2+4}{5}, \quad 0 < x < 1 \]

Given that $\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{11}{20},$ compute $\textrm{E}[2X-X^3+1].$

Hint: You may assume that $\textrm{E}[aX+bY] = a\textrm{E}[X] + b\textrm{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$
question.explanation:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

\begin{align*} \textrm{E} [2X-X^3+1] &= 2\textrm{E} [X] - \textrm{E} [X^3] + \textrm{E}[1] \\[5pt] &= 2\textrm{E} [X] - \textrm{E} [X^3] +1 \end{align*}

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

\[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

We already know $\textrm E [X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align*} \textrm{E}[X^3] &= \int_{0}^{1} x^3 \cdot \left( \dfrac{3x^2+4}{5} \right) \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( \dfrac{3}{5}x^5 + \dfrac{4}{5}x^3 \right) \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \left.\left( \dfrac{1}{10}x^6 + \dfrac{1}{5}x^4 \right)\right|_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{10} \end{align*}

Substituting $\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{11}{20}$ and $\textrm{E}[X^3] = \dfrac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \textrm{E}[2X-X^3+1] &= 2\textrm{E}[X] - \textrm{E}[X^3] + 1 \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot \dfrac{11}{20} - \dfrac{3}{10} + 1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{11}{10} - \dfrac{3}{10} + 1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{5}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\textrm E[10-4X^2].$

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^2}, \quad 1 < x < 2 \]
question.explanation:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value: \[ \textrm E[10-4X^2] = 10-4\textrm E[X^2] \]

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align*} \textrm E[X^2] &= \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{2} x^2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{x^2} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{2} 2\, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= 2x \, \Big|_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] &= 2 \end{align*}

Substituting $\textrm{E}[X^2] = 2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that \begin{align*} \textrm E[10 - 4X^2] &= 10 - 4\textrm E[X^2] \\[5pt] &= 10 - 4 \cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

question.text:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function: \[ f(x) = \dfrac{x}{4}, \quad 1 < x < 3 \] Given that $\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{13}{6},$ compute $\textrm{E}[X^2+6X+2].$

Hint: You may assume that $\textrm{E}[aX+bY] = a\textrm{E}[X] + b\textrm{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$
question.explanation:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value: \begin{align} \textrm E[X^2 + 6X+2] & = \textrm E[X^2] + 6\textrm E[X] + \textrm E[2]\\[5pt] & = \textrm E[X^2] + 6\textrm E[X] + 2 \end{align}

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

We already know $\textrm E [X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows: \begin{align*} \textrm E[X^2] &= \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^3 x^2 \cdot \dfrac{x}{4} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^3 \dfrac{x^3}{4} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \left. \dfrac{x^4}{16} \, \right|_{1}^3 \\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align*}

Substituting $\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{13}{6}$ and $\textrm{E}[X^2] = 5$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that \begin{align*} \textrm E[X^2+6X+2] &= \textrm E[X^2] + 6\textrm E[X] + 2 \\[5pt] &= 5 + 6\cdot \dfrac{13}{6} + 2\\[5pt] &= 5 + 13 + 2\\[5pt] &= 20. \end{align*}

question.text:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\textrm E[4X^2-3].$

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{x}{4}, \quad 1 < x < 3 \]
question.explanation:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

\[ \textrm E[4X^2-3] = 4 \textrm E[X^2] - 3 \]

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

\[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \textrm E[X^2] &= \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^3 x^2 \cdot \dfrac{x}{4} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^3\dfrac{x^3}{4} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \left. \dfrac{x^4}{16} \right|_{1}^3 \\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align*}

Substituting $\textrm{E}[X^2] = 5$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \textrm E[4X^2-3] &= 4 \textrm E[X^2] - 3 \\[3pt] &= 4 \cdot 5 - 3 \\[3pt] &= 17. \end{align*}

example.title: Computing the Mean of a Transformed Random Variable

question.text:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\textrm E[3X^2+4].$

\[ f(x) = 2-2x, \quad 0 < x < 1 \]
question.explanation:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value: \[ \textrm E[3X^2+4] = 3 \textrm E[X^2] + 4 \]

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by \[ \textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

\[\begin{align*} \textrm E[X^2] &= \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^1 x^2 \cdot (2 - 2x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^1 \left(2x^2 - 2x^3\right) \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \left. \left(\dfrac{2x^3}{3}- \dfrac{x^4}{2}\right) \right|_{0}^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{align*}\]

Substituting $\textrm{E}[X^2] = \dfrac{1}{6}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

\[\begin{align*} \textrm E[3X^2+4] &= 3 \textrm E[X^2] + 4 \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} + 4 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{2}. \end{align*}\]
